This is a feature request for deeper integration with the Neovim IDE. This falls under the extensibility area as it's about integrating with external tools. It's a valuable feature for a specific user group, so it has a medium priority.

Hi everyone! I wanted to share a Neovim integration I've been building for the Gemini CLI: **[gemini-cli.nvim](https://github.com/vaijab/gemini-cli.nvim)**.

It implements the MCP to turn Neovim into a semantic backend for the agent. Instead of just wrapping the terminal, it gives the model native access to:

*   **LSP & Tree-sitter Tools**: Accurate `Go to Definition`, `Find References`, and smart implementation extraction (including docstrings).
*   **Live Context Sync**: Automatically shares your active buffer, cursor position, and visual selections with the model.
*   **Native Diff Workflow**: Review and accept/reject proposed changes directly in a floating Neovim diff split.
*   **Diagnostic Awareness**: The agent can see and fix project errors using Neovim's diagnostic engine.

I ended up making my own mcp server in pure lua [`zaucy/mcp.nvim`](https://github.com/zaucy/mcp.nvim). I intentionally made it quite minimal. I extend it in my personal config. No lsp or diagnostics exposed. Tools can be registered by other plugins via `require('mcp').register_tool(...)`.

On top of that I made [`zaucy/gemini.nvim`](https://github.com/zaucy/gemini.nvim) That just registeres the minimal `openDiff` and `closeDiff` tools. I also added autocmds for the gemini hooks so you can respond to them in your own config.

Those two plugins + some of my custom config the workflow looks like this:

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/236dfcc4-b21d-4e5e-821a-ca4a180b8453)

You can see the diff in action and all the hooks being triggered right in neovim!

I believe this is also needed for React applications where streaming SSR emits content as hidden `div`s at the end of the HTML, with `script`s to move/copy things into place. I have sporadic strict mode violation errors due to Playwright matching the visible content _and also_ duplicated elements inside these hidden `div`s created by React. ``` Error: locator.fill: Error: strict mode violation: getByLabel('First name') resolved to 2 elements: 1) aka getByRole('textbox', { name: 'First name' }) 2) aka getByLabel('First name').nth(1) Call log: - waiting for getByLabel('First name') 44 | test('example', async ({ page }) => { 45 | await page.goto('/join'); > 46 | await page.getByLabel('First name').fill('Bear'); | ^ 47 | }); ``` In case it helps anyone else, I was able to workaround this using `getByRole` which excludes hidden elements by default (unlike `getByText` for example).

> I believe this is also needed for React applications where streaming SSR emits content as hidden divs at the end of the HTML

@OliverJAsh Thanks for the insights! My tests have been flaky for a while and I couldn't figure out the exact root cause. I suspected it was due to React hydration and elements somehow gets duplicated during a short transition time, and with your information I am able to confirm the tests were failed due to the hidden `divs`.

In my case I use `getByTestId` which is suppose to uniquely locate exact one element in my code, and the hidden elements are really confusing.

I think either this request to only select visible elements by default, or automatically wait to resolve strict mode violation (https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/issues/36045) would be helpful for the React use case. Alternatively, a config option to opt in for only select visible elements globally would work too.

I'd like to highlight that this feature request is about to become **significantly** more critical due to upcoming architectural shifts in the Next.js ecosystem.

As detailed in the [Next.js documentation](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/cache-components#navigation-uses-activity), when the [cacheComponents](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) flag is enabled the framework will now default to keeping previously visited routes in the DOM (marked as hidden/inert) rather than unmounting them.

In this new architecture, a simple navigation often results in two instances of the UI existing simultaneously in the DOM:
- The user-visible version.
- The cached, display: none version from the previous "activity."

Without a global configuration for visibility (as requested in this issue), developers adopting modern Next.js features will be forced to append .filter({ visible: true }) to **virtually every locator interaction** to avoid strict mode violations. This creates **massive boilerplate** and DX friction for what is effectively the "soon to be" default behavior of the framework.

Given that this "keep-alive" pattern is becoming a standard in modern web frameworks to enhance UX, Playwright needs a native, ergonomic way to handle "offscreen" or "inactive" subtrees without requiring verbose filtering on every line of test code.

I'd like to take a crack at this.

I plan to implement the `visibleOnly` parameter (alongside `strictSelectors`) with a default of `false`. This ensures backward compatibility and keeps the implementation lightweight/easy to review.

I don’t think this feature should be merged as-is. Moving a project only updates the project’s organization, but applications, compose stacks, and databases keep their references to servers (and registries, SSH keys, etc.). Those resources stay in the original organization, so the destination org would end up with a project that uses the source org’s servers and registries. That breaks organization isolation. Supporting move properly would require either restricting it to projects with no org-scoped resources, or handling servers/registries in the target org, which is a much larger change.

In our model, servers, registries, and SSH keys are scoped to an organization. Projects contain environments, and those contain applications, compose stacks, and databases—all of which reference servers (and applications also reference registries and SSH keys). When we “move” a project, we only change the project’s organizationId. We do not update the servers, registries, or other resources that the project’s services point to

 So after a move, the destination organization would own a project whose services still use servers (and registries, etc.) that belong to the source organization. That breaks the isolation we want between organizations.

For now, this is not something we want. It could lead to strange behaviour. I don't think we can proceed with this issue at the moment.

Our current thinking is that Bruno should always manage a default workspace. This removes friction for new users, since they don’t have to manually create one to get started. A workspace is essentially a directory that needs to follow a specific structure, and if the default workspace is placed at a custom location, the chances of that structure being accidentally modified, moved, or corrupted are relatively higher. When Bruno manages the default workspace itself, it can better ensure the structure remains intact and avoid situations where the workspace can no longer be opened correctly.

That said, users can still create custom workspaces at locations of their choice - for teams, projects, or general grouping of collections.

Building off of what @blagasse700  suggested with editing the `preferences.json` file, I tried something similar on mac using symlinks.

This is working well for me on two machines.

**Tested on:** macOS 14.8.1, macOS 15.7.5

1. Close Bruno.
2. Make sure your target workspace already has a valid `workspace.yml` (any existing Bruno workspace will have one).
3. Check the name of the default workspace folder inside `~/Library/Application Support/bruno/`. It's usually `default-workspace`, but may be `default-workspace-1` or similar depending on your install history.
4. Move or back up any collections from that folder if you want to keep them, then delete it.
5. Create a symlink in its place pointing to your workspace folder (**not the *workspace.yml* file**):

```bash
ln -s "/path/to/your/workspace" ~/Library/Application\ Support/bruno/default-workspace
```

6. Launch Bruno. Your workspace will open as the default, but the name will still display as "My Workspace".

I got podman working on rootless Podman with a few important flags:
- `SANDBOX_VOLUMES` env, with SELinux relabeling (`:Z`)
- ` --security-opt label=disable` to allow Podman socket mounting inside the container (see [RedHat blog](https://www.redhat.com/en/blog/podman-inside-container))

```bash
export OPENHANDS_VERSION=0.43
export OPENHANDS_RUNTIME=docker.all-hands.dev/all-hands-ai/runtime:$OPENHANDS_VERSION-nikolaik
export OPENHANDS_IMAGE=docker.all-hands.dev/all-hands-ai/openhands:$OPENHANDS_VERSION

FLAGS=(
  -it
  --rm
  -e "SANDBOX_RUNTIME_CONTAINER_IMAGE=$OPENHANDS_RUNTIME"
  # NOTE: `:Z` mount flag fixes SELinux permission errors
  -e "SANDBOX_VOLUMES=$PWD:/workspace:Z"
  -e LOG_LEVEL=debug
  -e DEBUG=true
  -e LOG_ALL_EVENTS=true
  # NOTE: Use Docker host env, but strip protocol prefix
  -v "${DOCKER_HOST#*://}:/var/run/docker.sock"

My repos live under `~/Work/<type>/<repo>` with a `.envrc` at each `~/Work/<type>/` that sets up that group's environment, and my herdr panes rely on direnv activating from the pane's cwd. So worktrees need to land under the same parent as their source repo — the central `~/.herdr/worktrees` default breaks that. I'm working around it today with per-repo symlinks plus a `realpath`-based `.envrc`, which is fragile and needs per-repo maintenance. The `{repo_parent}` placeholder proposed here would let me set `directory = "{repo_parent}/.herdr/worktrees"` and drop all of that.

For anyone who wants worktrees inside the repo without an extra tool: [herdr-repo-worktrees](https://github.com/tjs0/herdr-repo-worktrees) creates them at `<repo>/.worktrees/<name>` (configurable) through `herdr worktree create --path`, so they still group under the repo in the sidebar.
